content: Low back pain (LBP) is an extremely prevalent condition that most individuals experience at some point in their lives. It affects people across all age groups, including young adults, middle-aged individuals, and older adults. However, the prevalence and associated disability rates are highest among older adults. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued recommendations for various non-surgical interventions that should be included in the care of adults with chronic primary low back pain, including older adults. These guidelines also specify interventions that should not be routinely offered as part of standard care. Chronic primary low back pain, previously referred to as non-specific low back pain, is defined as pain lasting for more than three months that is not attributable to an underlying disease or other specific condition. This type of pain accounts for over 90% of chronic low back pain cases seen in primary care settings. Up to two-thirds of individuals who experience an acute episode of low back pain continue to have symptoms that persist for more than a year. These symptoms often follow a fluctuating course and are more commonly observed in older adults. Persistent symptoms are frequently associated with reduced physical and mental functioning, which negatively impacts quality of life, overall well-being, and the ability to engage in work and social activities. When planning and delivering care for adults with chronic primary low back pain, a comprehensive clinical assessment should be conducted from a biopsychosocial perspective. This assessment should be performed by a healthcare professional with the necessary expertise to determine appropriate interventions and identify cases requiring more detailed or urgent clinical review. Providing accurate and personalized information about chronic primary low back pain is essential. Personalized advice should help individuals understand their pain experience within a biopsychosocial framework and support their re-engagement in meaningful life activities. Care for chronic primary low back pain should involve a tailored package of interventions rather than relying on a single approach. The selection and sequencing of interventions should address the physical, psychological, and social factors contributing to the individual’s pain experience. Additionally, the person’s context, values, and preferences should be considered. Generally, care should begin with the least invasive and least potentially harmful interventions. The following non-surgical interventions are relevant for adults with chronic primary low back pain, including older adults, whether or not they have spine-related leg pain. These interventions are categorized based on their appropriateness for routine care: Interventions that may be offered as part of care: 1. Education: Structured and standardized education and advice. 2. Physical interventions: Structured exercise therapies or programs. 3. Psychological interventions: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). 4. Medicines: Topical capsaicin (Cayenne pepper), serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) antidepressants, and white willow (Salix spp.). Interventions that should not be used as part of routine care: 1. Physical interventions: Needling therapies, spinal manipulative therapy, massage, mobility assistive products, traction, therapeutic ultrasound, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), lumbar braces, belts, or supports. 2. Psychological interventions: Operant therapy. 3. Medicines: Opioid analgesics, tricyclic antidepressants, anticonvulsants, skeletal muscle relaxants, glucocorticoids, injectable local anesthetics, and Devil’s claw (Harpagophytum procumbens).
